events.text: A Hengshan disciple, a stiff young nun called Jingyu, stands at your door with a scroll. Hengshan offers a trade: the sword back, and they will publicly declare the curse nonsense, which will make your name a good deal less frightening.

effects.log: Jingyu takes the sword in both hands and bows very low. The curse is declared nonsense at a public ceremony.
Jingyu leaves without a word. The curse grows two more fires in the retelling.

ok.log: You win. Jingyu goes back to Hengshan with a lesson and no sword.

fail.log: She wins fairly and takes the sword back. It is somehow a relief.

events.text: The buyer of the Autumn Water sword, the salt merchant from Yangzhou, has had a run of very bad luck: a warehouse fire, a lawsuit, a son who ran off to be an actor. He believes in the curse completely. He would like you to take the sword back. He will pay.

effects.log: He pays you to take it. The curse is now the most profitable thing you own. (+100 taels)
You walk it up the mountain yourself. The elders do not know whether to arrest you or thank you, and do neither.
The merchant weeps. You leave before the sword can be handed over.

events.text: Coffin-maker Bo of Nanchang will, for 150 taels, build a coffin, hire mourners, find a bundle of reeds the right shape and hold the most convincing funeral the province has ever seen. 'For you,' he says, 'I would even weep myself. I am very good.'

effects.log: Bo starts measuring you at once, humming. (-150 taels)

ok.log: Bo agrees to 80, if he may keep the mourners' cakes. (-80 taels)

fail.log: Bo is offended and tells the coffin trade about it.

effects.log: You decide being alive is still worth something. Bo is disappointed.

events.text: Your funeral is magnificent. The Alliance sends a junior elder to confirm it, and he leaves relieved. Three rivals send wreaths; one sends fireworks. Coffin-maker Bo weeps for an hour. You watch it all from a teahouse window in a straw hat.

effects.log: You take a new name and a room above a dye shop. Nobody looks at you twice.

choices.text: Write to the rival who sent fireworks

effects.log: You send a single line: "Thank you for the fireworks." The rival leaves the province.
The stone says you were feared by all. Someone has left a bun on it. You eat it.

events.text: Being dead is peaceful, but it has drawbacks. Your old crew has broken up, your name is in a ballad instead of on a poster, and a young bandit in Jiangxi claims to be your ghost. People are leaving offerings at your grave, mostly cakes.

effects.log: You stay dead. It is the most restful thing you have ever done.
You walk into the Alliance's spring assembly. The junior elder faints.
You visit the grave every week at dusk. They are very good cakes.

events.text: The Black Wind Ridge bandits are leaderless: their chief fell off his own wall in the dark. Forty of them, a fort with a fine gate and no idea how to use it, are kneeling in the snow outside your inn, asking you to lead them. One of them is holding a goose as tribute.

effects.log: You ride up to the ridge with forty bandits and a goose. The fort is a mess.
You eat well that week. The bandits go home disappointed and argue about who keeps the next goose.

choices.text: Tell them to go home and farm

effects.log: Half of them actually do. The other half find a worse chief.

events.text: Black Wind Ridge under you is the best-run bandit fort in the north. The question is what to do with it: raid the Shanxi silver road, or turn the fort into a militia for the villages below, which suffer from other, worse bandits.

effects.log: The first raid is perfect. The silver road posts new guards the next week. (+200 taels)
The forty patrol the valley. The other bandits move to another province.
Raids in summer, patrols in winter. The villages are grateful in winter. (+100 taels)

events.text: The county magistrate rides up to Black Wind Ridge with a cart of rice and an offer: the fort can be the county's registered militia, banners and all, and the old bandit charges can quietly disappear. Your forty are stunned. One of them is weeping into the goose.

effects.log: The banners go up over the gate. The forty learn to salute, mostly with the right hand.
You keep the fort free and the valley safe. The magistrate leaves the rice anyway.

events.text: The Shanxi silver road has paid the Wudang sect, and twenty Wudang swordsmen are camped below Black Wind Ridge. Your forty bandits are looking at you, and at the back gate, and at you again.

ok.log: Wudang goes home. The ridge becomes the most feared fort in the north.

fail.log: Wudang takes the gate by noon. You are led down the ridge in a rope line with the others.

effects.log: The forty scatter into forty villages. You go west with the goose.

ok.log: Wudang agrees: the fort for forty pardons. They keep their word.

fail.log: Wudang agrees to the fort and not to the pardons.

events.text: A young woman in a stained plum robe collapses at your door: Lan, a Demonic Cult scribe who ran with a copy of the Cult's register of informers. The Cult wants her back, the Alliance wants the register, and she came to you because you are 'the only one both sides fear'.

effects.log: You put her in the cellar with a blanket and a lamp. She asks for paper.

choices.text: Sell the register to the Alliance

effects.log: The Alliance pays well. Lan disappears that night, and you never learn where. (+300 taels)
She goes back into the rain. You do not sleep well.

events.text: The Cult's hunters find your street within a month: three figures in plum, polite, unhurried, asking door to door about a scribe. Lan is in your cellar copying the register by lamplight because, she says, a second copy is always wise.

ok.log: The three in plum leave your street faster than they came, and do not come back.

fail.log: They take Lan from the cellar and leave you on the floor. The second copy is gone too.

choices.text: Smuggle her out to the coast

ok.log: A fish cart, a ferry, a salt boat. Lan reaches Quanzhou, and you come back alone.

fail.log: The hunters stop the fish cart. Lan runs, and you lose sight of her.

effects.log: The three in plum thank you very politely. Lan does not look back.

events.text: Lan has a new name and a stall writing letters for sailors in Quanzhou. She sends you the second copy of the register, sealed, with a note: 'Use it however you think best. I always wondered what you would choose.'

effects.log: The Alliance rounds up a dozen Cult informers in a month. Somebody, somewhere, toasts you.
It burns. A hundred people who never knew they were in danger sleep well.
You hide it under a floorboard. It is the most dangerous thing you own.

events.text: In Taiyuan a school for bounty hunters has opened, and its most popular course is about you: your routes, your habits, your favourite noodles. The headmaster, a retired hunter called Iron Crutch Yao, is looking for a guest lecturer who 'knows the subject'.

choices.text: Offer yourself as the lecturer, in a false beard

effects.log: Yao is delighted. Nobody else has offered.
You pay the fees in copper and sit in the third row.
You take the long road round Taiyuan, which is what the school teaches you would do.

events.text: Your lecture, 'The Mind of the Villain', is a sensation. You teach forty hunters that you always sleep facing the door and hate fish. Neither is true. Yao is thrilled and offers a second course. In the back row, one student takes very careful notes and keeps looking at your hands.

choices.text: Give a second course of lies

effects.log: Forty hunters graduate convinced you hate fish. You eat fish openly for years.
You leave in the night. The beard stays behind on the lectern.

choices.text: Have a word with the careful student

ok.log: She is a spy for a rival school, and only wanted your notes. You sell them to her.

fail.log: She runs straight to Yao. You leave by the window, with the beard.

events.text: As a student you do poorly on the paper about yourself. Iron Crutch Yao calls you in and explains, patiently, that the villain would never eat fish. You disagree. Yao fails you and recommends extra reading.

ok.log: You pass by writing down everything that is wrong about yourself. Yao calls it your best work.

fail.log: You fail again. Yao suggests another trade.

effects.log: You drop out and go to a fish restaurant to celebrate.

events.text: The Taiyuan school's graduates are everywhere now, and every one of them checks the fish markets last. Iron Crutch Yao has written a book from your lectures. It sells very well and is wrong on every page. He sends you a signed copy, 'to the kind lecturer with the beard'.

effects.log: You write a glowing review under a false name. Sales double.
You read a page a night. It is the funniest book you own.

events.text: The Yellow River dike at Huayuankou is cracking in the night rain, and the town below is asleep. The dike warden, a bent old man called Kang, runs along the top shouting for hands. He sees you, and he sees your poster on the wall of the dike house, and shouts for you anyway.

ok.log: You haul sandbags until dawn. The crack holds. Kang shakes your hand and does not let go.

fail.log: A section slips and takes you with it. You are pulled out half-drowned, and the rest holds.

effects.log: You hammer on every door in the lower town. By the time the water comes, the streets are empty.
You slip away in the rain. Behind you, the bells start ringing.

events.text: The constables know who held the dike at Huayuankou; half the town saw you. The county magistrate now has a problem: your poster on one wall of his yamen, and the town's petition for your pardon on the other. He has invited you to tea to discuss it.

ok.log: He takes down the poster with his own hands and gives it to you as a keepsake.

fail.log: The tea is good. The constables behind the screen are better.

effects.log: You send a polite letter. The poster comes down quietly a month later.
You stay away. The petition and the poster go on sharing a wall.

events.text: Warden Kang has died, and the town has raised a stone at the dike with the names of everyone who worked that night. Yours is there, third from the top, carved deep. Someone keeps scratching it out. Someone else keeps carving it back in.

effects.log: You recut every stroke one night. In the morning it is scratched again, and recut by noon.
You leave it. Both of them keep at it for years, and the stone wears thin there.

events.text: The Alliance has caught your old lookout, Sparrow Lin, a cheerful thief who never hurt anyone and talks too much. They will trade her for you, or for the jade seal of Emei you took last year. The exchange is at the Moon Lake pavilion, on the full moon.

effects.log: You hand over the seal. Sparrow Lin walks out of the pavilion talking.
You walk into the pavilion. Sparrow Lin walks out, and keeps looking back.
You study the lake for a month. It is very wide.

events.text: Moon Lake at the full moon: a stone pavilion on the water, six Alliance swordsmen, and Sparrow Lin in the middle eating a pear and complaining about the food. She sees you on the far shore and waves, which ruins any plan that involved surprise.

ok.log: You come up out of the water behind the swordsmen. Lin is already running.

fail.log: The water is cold and the swordsmen are dry. You join Lin in the cell.

ok.log: The six swordsmen are bored, cold and badly paid. They let her go for a promise.

fail.log: They let you talk, and then keep you too.

choices.text: Give up the seal after all

effects.log: You throw the seal across the water. Lin catches it, hands it over, and walks out.

events.text: Sparrow Lin has decided she owes you her life and has followed you ever since, talking. She has told the inn, the ferry, two monks and a constable about the rescue at Moon Lake. The constable is taking notes.

effects.log: You buy her a teahouse stall. She talks to customers all day and is very happy. (-40 taels)

ok.log: She learns to be silent for an hour at a time. It is a miracle.

fail.log: She tells the constable about the lessons.

effects.log: Every inn in the county knows the Moon Lake story, with you as the hero.

events.text: Emei sends a nun to thank you for the seal's return, which is awkward, since you stole it. The nun is very polite. 'The Abbess says one who gives back is halfway home,' she says, and leaves before you can ask where the other half is.

effects.log: The Abbess serves you tea on the mountain and tells you. It takes all afternoon.
You laugh. The nun, at the bottom of the stairs, laughs too.

events.text: Someone in your crew is selling your plans to the Alliance. Three jobs in a row have found constables waiting. It could be Old Hou the cook, Silk Ning who keeps the books, or young Thirteen who runs messages and hums all the time.

choices.text: Feed each one a different false plan

ok.log: The constables turn up at the canal, which was the plan you told Silk Ning.

fail.log: The constables turn up at all three places. It is not just one of them.

effects.log: You send them all away. The jobs go badly without a cook, a bookkeeper or a messenger.

ok.log: Silk Ning puts down her brush and says, "It was me."

fail.log: Old Hou throws a ladle at you for asking. Nobody confesses.

events.text: Silk Ning does not run. She sits at the books and explains, in her flat voice, that the Alliance holds her brother in a Luoyang cell and has promised him out if she gives them three more jobs. She has given them two.

ok.log: The Alliance raids an empty warehouse, and keeps its word. The brother walks out.

fail.log: The Alliance sees through it. The brother stays in the cell.

effects.log: She goes without a word. You learn later that she went straight to Luoyang.

ok.log: You bring the brother out over the cell roof. Ning weeps for the first time anyone has seen.

fail.log: You end up in the cell next to his.

events.text: Silk Ning's brother is a shy seal-carver who cannot stop thanking you. Ning herself is back at the books, keeping two sets: one for you, one marked 'what we owe', with the names of people the crew has hurt. 'In case you ever want it,' she says.

effects.log: Ning crosses off the first name with great satisfaction. (-100 taels)
She watches it burn and starts a new one the next day.
You keep both on the shelf, side by side. Sometimes you read the second.

events.text: Elder Huang of the Kongtong sect hunted you for twenty years and never caught you. Now he is dying in a guest house in Lanzhou, and his disciple has come under a white flag: the old man wants to see you before he goes. 'He says it is not a trap,' the disciple adds, 'and he would know.'

effects.log: You ride to Lanzhou with the disciple, who does not speak once.
You write a page. The disciple carries it back, and Huang has it read to him twice.
You go west. Huang dies laughing, the disciple says later.

events.text: Elder Huang is a small, yellow, cheerful old man under a quilt. 'Twenty years,' he says. 'I always wanted to ask: the Fenzhou granary, the year of the locusts. Was it you?' It was not. It was the only thing on his list you did not do.

effects.log: He laughs until he coughs. "Twenty years," he says. "Twenty years for the wrong granary."

choices.text: Say it was you, to give him the satisfaction

effects.log: He nods, satisfied, and holds your hand for an hour.
He thinks a long time. "Not stopping for lunch more often," he says.

events.text: Elder Huang's funeral in Lanzhou is small and full of Kongtong swordsmen who look at you as if you had come into the wrong house. His disciple hands you a box. Inside is a sealed letter to the Martial Alliance, in Huang's hand, about you.

ok.log: It asks the Alliance to stop hunting you. Out of respect for Huang, they mostly do.

fail.log: It names three of your crimes in loving detail. The Alliance is very grateful to Huang.

effects.log: It asks the Alliance to leave you be. You reseal it badly and deliver it anyway.
You burn it without reading. Some questions should stay with the dead.

events.text: The Hundred Flowers Pavilion in Luoyang publishes its list of the Ten Great Evils every spring, and the murim reads it like the court gazette. This year you are seventh, between a poisoner nobody has seen and a pirate who is probably dead. You feel you deserve better.

effects.log: You have a busy year. The compilers take note.

choices.text: Pay the compilers to drop you

effects.log: The compilers take the silver with great dignity. (-100 taels)
Seventh is a fine number. You go back to your noodles.

events.text: You are third this year, and the second and first have sent invitations: a meeting of the Great Evils on a lake island, to divide the country into hunting grounds. The poisoner says the tea will be safe. The pirate has written back from what is definitely a grave.

ok.log: You come away with the richest province and a cup you never drank from. (+200 taels)

fail.log: The tea was not safe. You spend a month recovering, and the province goes to someone else.

choices.text: Send the invitation to the Alliance

effects.log: The Alliance is very interested in the lake island. You are not on it.
You decline politely. The poisoner sends a cake anyway. You do not eat it.

events.text: The compilers took your silver and dropped you from the Ten Great Evils, and the murim has noticed the gap more than it ever noticed the name. The new edition carries a footnote: 'Seventh last year: whereabouts and reasons unknown.' Teahouses argue about it nightly.

effects.log: The footnote becomes more famous than the list. Nobody knows your face.
You get back on at fourth. The compilers keep the silver.

events.text: The lake island meeting did not end as the Great Evils intended: the Alliance had a spy in the kitchen. The first Great Evil is in a cell, the second has vanished, and you are now first on the list, which nobody can remember wanting.

effects.log: First. The compilers send a congratulatory scroll, which is very strange to receive.
You go quiet for a year, then two. By the third edition you are a footnote.

events.text: The Martial Alliance is trying you in your absence at Mount Song: the full tribunal, nine elders, a crowd of three thousand, and an empty chair in the middle where you are supposed to sit. The verdict is expected to be death. The chair is a nice one, red lacquer.

choices.text: Walk in and sit in the chair

effects.log: Three thousand people go silent. The chief elder drops his brush.

ok.log: Your defence is read aloud and is so elegant that two elders vote to acquit on style alone.

fail.log: Your defence is read aloud. The crowd laughs at the third line.

effects.log: They sentence the empty chair to death. It is carried out on a cart.

events.text: The trial at Mount Song has run for a season, because nobody planned for you to actually come. The elders cannot agree whether arresting someone sitting in the defendant's chair counts as an ambush. Today the witnesses speak.

ok.log: Witness after witness gets the dates wrong. The elders begin to look embarrassed.

fail.log: The witnesses have the dates right. Guilty, and three years in the Alliance cells.

effects.log: The crowd is silent for a long time. The sentence is three years, not death.

ok.log: You stand up, bow, and walk out through three thousand people. Nobody stops you.

fail.log: Somebody stops you.

events.text: The verdict: guilty of eleven charges, not guilty of twenty-six, and the chief elder adds a line nobody has heard before: 'the defendant is advised to go home.' The Alliance will hunt you less now; some of its elders are embarrassed. One sends you the red chair.

effects.log: It sits by your door. Everyone who visits asks to sit in it.

choices.text: Take the advice and go home

effects.log: You go home and stay there. It is surprisingly pleasant.

events.text: The Inn of Three Rivers, high on the Wuling road, has one rule carved over the door: no blades drawn under this roof. Heroes and villains both drink here. Tonight the only empty seat is beside an Emei swordswoman who has your poster folded in her sleeve.

effects.log: She looks at you, at the poster, at the carving over the door, and pours you a cup.
You drink at the counter with a salt smuggler who snores.
You sleep on the road in the rain. The inn's lanterns stay lit all night.

events.text: The Emei swordswoman, Sister Qiu, is back at the Inn of Three Rivers, and so are you, by an accident that keeps happening. You have never fought; you have drunk a dozen pots of tea. Tonight she says the Emei abbess has ordered her to follow you out of the inn tomorrow.

ok.log: You go out through the kitchen at dawn. She is waiting at the front door, and smiles when she hears.

fail.log: She is waiting at the kitchen door. The fight on the road is short and very polite.

choices.text: Ask her what she will do

effects.log: 'Follow you,' she says. 'The abbess said nothing about catching.' She walks beside you to the next town and turns back.

choices.text: Stay at the inn another month

effects.log: Neither of you leaves. The innkeeper is delighted. (-40 taels)

events.text: A year on, the innkeeper hands you a letter from Sister Qiu: Emei found out she lost your trail on purpose, and sent her to keep a shrine on Mount Emei for three years. 'It is very quiet,' she writes. 'Come and drink tea. No blades drawn under that roof either.'

effects.log: You climb for three days. She has the tea ready, as if she knew the hour.
You write back about the inn, the rain and the snoring smuggler. She writes back about the shrine. It goes on for years.

events.text: You go back to the village you grew up in, for the first time since your name went up on the posters. The well, the pagoda tree, the dye-maker's vats are all where they were. The people are too. They all find somewhere else to be as you walk down the street.

effects.log: The schoolhouse smells of ink and damp. Your name is still carved on the third bench.

choices.text: Sit at the well until someone talks

ok.log: The dye-maker comes for water at dusk and says, "You were always trouble." It is almost warm.

fail.log: Nobody comes to the well all day. The village goes without water rather than talk.

effects.log: You walk out before the pagoda tree. You do not look back until the hill.

events.text: Old Teacher Xue, who taught you characters with a willow switch, is still alive and nearly blind. You have come back again, and this time he knows your voice at the gate. 'The worst student I had,' he says. 'And now the most famous. Sit down. Read me something.'

ok.log: You read him Du Fu. He mouths the words with you and corrects nothing.

fail.log: He corrects every tone, delighted, exactly as he used to.

effects.log: He laughs until he coughs. "You always did bad characters," he says.

choices.text: Ask what the village says of you

effects.log: He tells you, all of it. It is worse than the posters and kinder in one place.

events.text: Teacher Xue has died, and his will asks that the school be kept open, and names you, of all people, to pay for it. The village is outraged. It is also poor. The headman comes to see what you will do, carrying the will at arm's length.

effects.log: The school stays open. The children are told only that it was Teacher Xue's will. (-150 taels)

choices.text: Teach there yourself for a season

effects.log: You teach characters badly and swordplay not at all. The children love it.
The school closes. The village has one more reason, and it was not short of them.

events.text: Plague in the walled town of Xinye, and the governor's soldiers have closed the roads around it. Nobody goes in, and no medicine either. An herbalist, Mother Qin, has a cart of fever bark and no way through. 'They are afraid of the plague,' she says. 'They are more afraid of you.'

choices.text: Drive the cart up and let them see your face

ok.log: The soldiers look at your face and step back from the barrier. The cart rolls through.

fail.log: One of them loses his nerve and looses a bolt. The cart goes through anyway, with the bolt in your arm.

choices.text: Take the bark and sell it

effects.log: Fever bark sells very high in a plague year. Mother Qin's face stays with you longer than the silver. (+150 taels)

ok.log: You lead the cart through a dry stream bed at night and in by a drain gate.

fail.log: The path is watched now. Mother Qin goes back to the road to wait.

events.text: Inside Xinye, the plague has broken. The town is thin and grey but alive, and Mother Qin has slept in the temple with the sick for a season. The governor's soldiers at the gate now want to arrest you, but the townspeople have barred the gate from inside.

effects.log: You stay. The gate stays barred, and the soldiers, eventually, go home.
You go over the south wall at night. Somebody has left a bag of millet at the bottom.

choices.text: Surrender so the gate can open

effects.log: You walk out to the soldiers. The town opens its gate behind you, and the carts go in.

events.text: The people of Xinye have built a small shrine to Mother Qin, who caught the fever in its last week. Behind her figure is a second one, holding the reins of a cart, with a scarf over its face. The town voted on what to call it. They chose 'The Driver'.

effects.log: You light incense for Mother Qin. A child tells you the story of The Driver, and gets most of it right.
You never tell anyone. It is the only thing you have done that you keep entirely to yourself.

events.text: The Cult's Left Envoy sends down an order: the village of Stone Pear sheltered an orthodox spy, and it is to burn by the new moon as a lesson. The order is in red ink, which in the Cult means there will be no second letter. The spy, everyone knows, left a month ago.

effects.log: You give the village one night. They flee with what they can carry, and Stone Pear burns behind them.

choices.text: Warn the village and burn only empty houses

ok.log: The smoke is seen from the Cult's watchtower. Nobody in it learns the houses were empty.

fail.log: The Left Envoy's watcher sees the villagers leaving before the fire. He reports it.

effects.log: You send the red letter back with nothing written on it. That is an answer too.

events.text: A black lacquer token arrives: you are to appear in the Hall of Judgement on Black Wood Cliff. Those who refuse a red order are rarely seen again. Those who run from the Cult are always hunted.

ok.log: You argue that burning an empty village teaches nothing. The Heavenly Demon laughs, and the matter is dropped.

fail.log: The Hall is not persuaded. You leave Black Wood Cliff alive, and slowly.

effects.log: You go to the coast and take a fisherman's name. The token stays on the table.

choices.text: Go straight to the Left Envoy

ok.log: The Left Envoy is not seen in the Hall after that. Nobody sends you red ink again.

fail.log: The Left Envoy is very strong. You are thrown out of the hall and down most of the stairs.

events.text: Stone Pear has been rebuilt five li downstream, and the villagers have a new custom: on the new moon each year they leave every door open all night, so that whoever comes will see nobody is hiding anything. A child on the road asks you if that keeps a fire away.

effects.log: The child nods, satisfied. You walk on, and do not look at the doors.
You carry beams for a month. Nobody asks who you are. Everybody knows.
You walk on. The doors stand open behind you all night.

events.text: You kneel at the gate of the Taiji Hall on Wudang, in plain clothes, your blade wrapped and laid on the step, and ask to be taken in as the lowest of servants. The gate disciple goes pale and runs. An hour later an elder comes down, looks at you, and says one word: 'No.'

effects.log: You kneel until dark, and through the night. In the morning the step is wet with dew and you are still there.

ok.log: 'Because you came for yourself,' the elder says. You kneel down again to think about it.

fail.log: He does not answer. The disciples whisper about it for a month.

effects.log: You pick up the blade and go down the mountain. It is heavier than it was.

events.text: You came back with the spring and knelt again, and again, and the disciples have stopped running; one leaves you rice. Today the Wudang elder, Master Yun, sits down on the step beside you. 'The people you hurt cannot get in here either,' he says. 'Why should you?'

choices.text: Leave the mountain and go to them

effects.log: You stand up, bow to Master Yun, and walk down the mountain toward the first name on your list.

ok.log: He sighs for a long time, and then opens the gate. You carry water for Wudang for a year.

fail.log: He shakes his head and goes back up. The rain starts again.

effects.log: You give up. On the way down you pass a hunter going up, with your poster.

events.text: Three years of going door to door with what you owe. Some doors opened; most did not. Then a letter from Wudang, from Master Yun: 'The gate is open now, if you still want it. I suspect you no longer need it.'

effects.log: You climb the steps you knelt on. Master Yun is waiting, and pours the tea himself.

choices.text: Write back thanks and stay on the road

effects.log: You write back one line: "You were right." There are more doors to knock on.

events.text: Grandfather Liu left the house three things: a leaking roof, two mu of millet, and an ox called Old Thunder. Now Cousin Liu Gen and Aunt Peng stand in your yard, each with a hand on the ox, and Old Thunder is eating your fence.

choices.text: Keep the ox. The head of the house keeps the plough.

effects.log: You lead Old Thunder into your shed. By sundown Aunt Peng has told the whole village you are a miser.

choices.text: Share it: each claimant has the ox two days in six.

effects.log: Nobody is pleased, everyone agrees, and Old Thunder gets three times the bran.

choices.text: Let the ox choose. Three buckets of bran, three claimants.

ok.log: Old Thunder walks past both of them and puts its nose in your bucket. Nobody argues with an ox.

fail.log: Old Thunder eats from all three buckets and lies down. Nobody wins, so everybody shares.

events.text: Spring ploughing. The rains came late, and every field in the valley must be turned in the same ten days. One ox, three fields. Cousin Liu Gen was seen at dawn by your shed with a rope over his shoulder.

choices.text: Plough your own field first. You are the head.

effects.log: Your millet goes in on time and pays well. Two other fields go in late, and two people remember. (+30 taels)

choices.text: Plough Aunt Peng's field first. She is the oldest.

effects.log: Aunt Peng brings you a basket of eggs and stops calling you a miser, mostly.

choices.text: Yoke yourself beside the ox and plough all three by moonlight.

ok.log: Three fields in nine nights. The valley starts calling you 'the second ox', with respect.

fail.log: You fall asleep in a furrow on the fourth night. The fields get done anyway, slowly.

events.text: Old Thunder lies down in the straw and will not get up. The horse doctor from Three Willows says the ox is simply old. A butcher's cart has already stopped at the gate, and the butcher offers 40 taels.

choices.text: Sell. Forty taels is a new roof.

effects.log: The cart creaks away. The roof stops leaking, and the yard is very quiet. (+40 taels)

choices.text: Pay the horse doctor to try his bitter mash (-25 taels).

ok.log: Old Thunder gets up on the third day and eats a basket. The doctor takes the credit. (-25 taels)

fail.log: The mash does nothing, but the ox goes easy, warm, in its own straw. (-25 taels)

choices.text: Send the butcher off. Sit up with Old Thunder and the other two claimants.

effects.log: Three claimants sit in a shed all night with one old ox. Somewhere near dawn, Aunt Peng starts telling stories about Grandfather Liu.

events.text: The spring after Old Thunder, Cousin Liu Gen comes up the road leading a red calf on a rope. 'Bought it in Three Willows,' he says. 'Half from me, half from Aunt Peng. It is the house's. You are the house.'

choices.text: Name the calf Little Thunder and give Liu Gen the first ploughing.

effects.log: The calf is stubborn and greedy and the whole family loves it. The house is a house again.

choices.text: Pay them back their share, so the calf is truly yours (-20 taels).

effects.log: Liu Gen looks a little hurt, then pockets the silver. The calf does not care whose it is. (-20 taels)

events.text: A year on, the village still calls your yard 'the ox house', and not kindly. Aunt Peng ploughs with a hired mule now. Cousin Liu Gen has stopped coming to the new year meal.

choices.text: Carry a jar of wine to Liu Gen's door and say you were wrong.

effects.log: He makes you stand in the cold a while, then lets you in. The jar is empty by midnight.

choices.text: Let them sulk. A head of house cannot be loved by everyone.

effects.log: The fields are yours and the silence is yours too. You get used to both.

events.text: The counting house holds two ledgers for the same ten years. One shows the shop in profit. The other, in the hand of the sibling who contests the seat, shows a hole of 600 taels. The partners meet in three days to choose a head.

choices.text: Sit up three nights and check every line yourself.

ok.log: Line by line you find it: the hole is real, and it was dug years before either of you held a brush.

fail.log: By the third dawn the numbers swim. You know only that one of the ledgers is lying.

choices.text: Pay old clerk Fan to tell you which ledger is true (-40 taels).

effects.log: Fan bites the silver and talks: the hole is your late patriarch's, a debt to the salt office he never told anyone about. (-40 taels)

choices.text: Burn the second ledger before the partners see it.

effects.log: Ten years of numbers curl up in the stove. You feel lighter, and then not.

events.text: The partners sit around the long table: Master Ou of the silk guild, the widow Tang who owns a third of the warehouses, and two men who say nothing and count everything. Both ledgers, or one, lie between you.

choices.text: Show them the hole, and who dug it, and offer a plan to fill it.

ok.log: The widow Tang taps the plan twice and says, 'This one.' The partners nod. The seat is yours.

fail.log: Master Ou says the plan is young. The partners want another year to think.

choices.text: Say the shop should go to whoever can fill the hole, and step back.

effects.log: The sibling who contests the seat takes the hole and the shop together. You keep your name clean and your hands empty.

choices.text: Swear the second ledger is a forgery.

ok.log: You swear well. The partners believe you, and the hole is still there.

fail.log: Clerk Fan coughs at the wrong moment. Nobody at the table trusts either of you now.

events.text: The partners sit around the long table, and only one ledger lies on it: yours. The sibling who contests the seat stares at the ash still in the stove and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Take the vote. The ledger says profit.

effects.log: The partners vote for the ledger they can see. The seat is yours, and so is the hole you hid. (+60 taels)

choices.text: Confess the burning before the vote.

effects.log: The widow Tang looks at you for a long time. 'Honest too late,' she says, and votes against you.

events.text: Behind the third ancestral tablet, Aunt Wei finds a will no one has seen before. It names the sibling who contests the seat as heir, in a hand very like your late patriarch's. The ink, you notice, still smells faintly of pine.

choices.text: Ask to see the will in daylight.

ok.log: In daylight the seal is a fraction too small, and the paper is from this year's mill.

fail.log: It looks right to you. That is the trouble with a good forgery.

choices.text: Take the will to the scribe in the market who copies seals (-30 taels).

effects.log: The scribe turns pale, then honest: he carved the seal himself, last spring, for a customer in a grey hood. (-30 taels)

choices.text: Write a will of your own and hide it behind the fourth tablet.

effects.log: Now there are two wills behind the tablets, and the ancestors have a great deal to think about.

events.text: The household gathers in the hall at the new moon to read the will aloud. Aunt Wei holds it. The incense burns straight up, which the old women say means the ancestors are listening.

choices.text: Lay the proof before the tablets and let everyone see the false seal.

effects.log: The hall goes silent, then loud. The false will is burnt before the tablets, and the seat is yours by right.

choices.text: Keep the proof in your sleeve. Offer the sibling a way out in private.

effects.log: The will is quietly 'found to be damaged'. The seat is yours, and nobody else ever knows why it was given up.

events.text: The household gathers in the hall at the new moon. Aunt Wei reaches behind the tablets and comes back with two wills, one in each hand. Everyone looks at you, and then at the sibling who contests the seat.

choices.text: Insist yours is the true one.

ok.log: Aunt Wei chooses yours. You win the seat, and the ancestors' tablets seem to look away.

fail.log: Your ink is too fresh. The house hands the seat to the other forger, who at least forged first.

choices.text: Laugh, tear both wills in half, and ask for a vote.

effects.log: The elders are so startled they agree. The vote is put off to the spring.

events.text: Uncle Zhao Heng ran the clan while you were young, and he has not noticed you grew up. The clan seal is still in his sleeve, the stewards still bring him the accounts, and at meals he still cuts your meat.
events.arc: The Regent Who Would Not Go

choices.text: Ask him for the seal, politely, at dinner.

ok.log: He laughs, pats your hand, and says, 'Next year.' But the whole table heard you ask.

fail.log: He talks over you about the price of rice. The stewards look at their bowls.

choices.text: Start reading the accounts yourself at night.

effects.log: The accounts are neat. Too neat. Every year the clan's grain store is a little smaller.

choices.text: Leave it. He has done well by the clan.

effects.log: You let another year go by under Uncle Zhao's sleeve.

events.text: At the spring rites, Uncle Zhao Heng stands where the head of the clan stands, and lights the first incense. The elders look at you. A year ago they would not have.
events.arc: The Regent Who Would Not Go

choices.text: Step up beside him and light the second stick from his.

effects.log: Two heads at one altar. The elders whisper, and some of them smile.

choices.text: Ask the elders, in front of everyone, whose rite this is.

ok.log: Elder Mo clears his throat and says, 'The heir's.' Uncle Zhao's hand shakes as he passes you the taper.

fail.log: Nobody answers. Uncle Zhao finishes the rite and does not look at you for a month.

choices.text: Let him finish. Talk to him alone after.

effects.log: That night he tells you about the year the river took the east fields, and how close the clan came to nothing.

events.text: The grain store is a third smaller than the accounts say. Steward Kou admits it in a whisper: Uncle Zhao Heng has been feeding a second household in the hills for twenty years. Nobody knows whose.
events.arc: The Regent Who Would Not Go

choices.text: Ride to the hills and see for yourself.

effects.log: In the hills you find a widow and six orphans of the river year, the families of men who drowned saving the clan's dyke.

choices.text: Lay the accounts before the elders.

effects.log: The elders take the seal from Uncle Zhao's sleeve that same night and put it in yours.

events.text: Uncle Zhao Heng comes to your room with the clan seal wrapped in red cloth. 'I held it too long,' he says. 'Holding things is all I know.' His hands are old now. You had not noticed that either.
events.arc: The Regent Who Would Not Go

choices.text: Take it, and ask him to stay on as your counsellor.

effects.log: He grumbles for a week and advises you for ten years. The clan has never been better run.

choices.text: Take it, and send him to rest in the hill house with a pension (-60 taels).

effects.log: He goes. The household in the hills gets a second old man to feed and a good one. (-60 taels)

choices.text: Tell him to keep it one more year, with you beside him.

effects.log: He weeps, which nobody has ever seen. The year goes quickly.

events.text: Steward Bai has served this house for fifty-one years. He knows where the good silver is buried, which ancestor owed which debt, and who really broke the blue vase. He bows to you the same way he bowed to the head before you, which is to say, barely.

choices.text: Ask him to teach you the house.

effects.log: He looks at you for a long moment, then hands you a key you did not know existed.

choices.text: Remind him who is head now.

effects.log: He bows lower. The tea is cold for a month.

choices.text: Give him a raise and hope for the best (-30 taels).

effects.log: He accepts it the way a mountain accepts rain. (-30 taels)

events.text: A creditor arrives with a paper for 200 taels, signed, he says, by the head before you. Steward Bai stands behind your chair and says nothing. He coughs, once.

choices.text: Turn and ask Steward Bai what the cough meant.

effects.log: 'That debt was paid at the Dragon Boat festival twelve years ago,' he says. 'I have the receipt.' The creditor leaves you 20 taels for the trouble. (+20 taels)

choices.text: Pay it. A house honours its dead (-200 taels).

effects.log: You pay. Later Steward Bai mutters that it was paid already. (-200 taels)

choices.text: Refuse and send for the magistrate.

ok.log: The creditor's paper does not survive the magistrate's magnifying glass.

fail.log: The magistrate wants a fee to read anything. (-10 taels)

events.text: Steward Bai is dying, slowly and with great dignity, in the small room behind the kitchen. He asks for you, only you. 'There is one thing about this house I never told anyone,' he says.

effects.log: Under the old well, a box: the house's emergency silver, buried in the year of the bandits. He makes you swear to spend it only on the house. (+120 taels)

choices.text: Tell him to keep his secret and rest.

effects.log: He smiles for the first time in fifty-one years. 'Good,' he says. 'The house is in the right hands.'

events.text: Steward Bai retires to his nephew's village with one bag and a lifetime of other people's secrets. At the gate he hands you a ledger of his own: every crack in the house, in his small grey hand.

effects.log: The east wall needs pinning, the cook is honest, and your great-uncle was a terrible poet. The house makes sense at last.

choices.text: Walk him to the village, carrying his bag.

effects.log: It takes a whole day. He tells you who broke the blue vase. It was the head before you.

events.text: Matchmaker Hong arrives in a sedan chair with an offer from the Gu house of Linan: their heir, a betrothal, and the Gu silk trade behind whichever of you holds the seat. The sibling who contests the seat has already been sent a copy.

choices.text: Accept the betrothal at once. The Gu silk will win the house.

effects.log: Matchmaker Hong beams. The Gu house sends a jade hairpin and a very long list of conditions.

choices.text: Go to Linan and meet the Gu heir before deciding (-30 taels).

effects.log: The Gu heir is clever, tired and frank: 'They want a seat-holder, not a person. So do yours.' (-30 taels)

choices.text: Refuse. A seat won by betrothal is not a seat.

effects.log: Matchmaker Hong's sedan chair turns around and goes straight to the sibling who contests the seat.

events.text: The house elders meet in the long hall to choose a head. Nobody mentions the Gu house, and every one of them has already heard what the Gu silk trade is worth: nine thousand bolts a year.

choices.text: Bring the Gu letter to the elders.

effects.log: The Gu silk tips the elders. The seat is yours, and so is a betrothal you did not entirely choose. (+80 taels)

choices.text: Tell the elders you will not be won with silk, and ask for a fair vote.

ok.log: Elder Shen likes the answer. So do most of the others. The seat is yours, with no strings of silk.

fail.log: The elders choose to wait a year. Nobody likes to vote against silk.

events.text: You and the Gu heir write to each other over the season. In the last letter: 'If we both refuse, neither house can use us. I will refuse if you will.'

choices.text: Refuse together, and stand for the seat on your own.

effects.log: The two refusals arrive on the same day. Both houses are furious. You have a friend in Linan for life.

choices.text: Accept after all, and let the Gu heir down gently.

effects.log: The silk comes, the seat comes, and one letter from Linan comes, very short. (+60 taels)

events.text: The sibling who contests the seat accepted the Gu betrothal, and now sits at the head of the table with Gu silk on every cushion. The elders are counting bolts. You have one move left.

choices.text: Go to the Gu house yourself and tell them what the sibling is really like.

ok.log: The Gu house withdraws its offer. The silk is carted away, and the elders turn back to you.

fail.log: The Gu house thanks you for your concern and doubles the silk.

choices.text: Bow out with grace, and wish them a happy marriage.

effects.log: You give up the seat at the betrothal feast and raise the first cup. Everyone agrees it was very well done.

events.text: The clan elders have decided: three tasks, set by Grand-aunt Lan, who is ninety-two and fond of riddles. Whoever wins two takes the seat. The first: carry water from the Black Spring to the ancestral basin without spilling a drop.

choices.text: Run the mountain path with the bucket.

ok.log: You arrive first, the water still as a mirror. Grand-aunt Lan nods once.

fail.log: You slip on the moss and arrive with half a bucket. The other bucket is full.

choices.text: Walk slowly and carry the spring in a sealed jar instead.

effects.log: 'Nobody said bucket,' you say. Grand-aunt Lan laughs until she has to sit down. The task is yours.

choices.text: Stop to give water to the old porter collapsed on the path.

effects.log: You arrive last with an empty bucket. The porter, it turns out, was Grand-aunt Lan's grandson.

events.text: The second task: Grand-aunt Lan gives each of you 50 taels and a month. 'Bring me back more,' she says. 'Any honest way.' The cousins start guessing at once, and the porter from the mountain path writes the guesses down.

choices.text: Buy cheap pears in the hills and sell them in town.

ok.log: You come back with 110 taels and a sore back. The other purse holds 90. (+20 taels)

fail.log: The pears rot in the summer heat. You come back with 40, and the shame of it. (-10 taels)

choices.text: Give the 50 taels to the village school and bring back the schoolmaster's thanks.

effects.log: Grand-aunt Lan reads the thank-you letter twice and puts it in her sleeve without a word.

choices.text: Bring back exactly 50 taels and a list of every honest trade that failed you.

effects.log: 'At least you did not lie,' says Grand-aunt Lan. The task goes to the other purse.

events.text: The third task is a question. Grand-aunt Lan asks it of both of you before the whole clan, with the incense lit and the porter from the mountain path sitting at the back: 'What is the clan for?'

effects.log: The old men nod. The young cousins look disappointed. Grand-aunt Lan writes something down.

choices.text: 'For the people who cannot carry water up a mountain.'

effects.log: There is a long silence. Then the porter at the back of the hall starts to clap.

choices.text: 'I do not know yet. Let me hold the seat ten years and I will tell you.'

effects.log: Grand-aunt Lan laughs for the second time this year, which the clan considers a sign.

events.text: Grand-aunt Lan unrolls her paper before the ancestral tablets. She has kept her own score, as it turns out, and her score has very little to do with buckets.

effects.log: 'Two of three,' she says, 'and the third one I liked.' The clan seal is placed in your hands.

choices.text: Bow to the sibling who contests the seat before she can speak.

effects.log: You give the seat up before it can be given to you. Grand-aunt Lan tears up her paper and nobody ever learns what was on it.

events.text: Grand-aunt Lan unrolls her paper before the ancestral tablets and reads the score aloud, task by task, slowly, because she is ninety-two and she has earned the right to make people wait.

ok.log: 'The seat goes to the one who brought the spring in a jar,' she says. 'Or the pears. I forget which. Both of them are you.'

fail.log: The score is even. Grand-aunt Lan says she will think about it, and falls asleep in her chair.

choices.text: Ask for a fourth task: a duel before the tablets.

roll.foeName: the sibling who contests the seat

ok.log: The duel is short and clean. You lower your sword first, and the clan seal is yours.

fail.log: You are on the flagstones before you have drawn a full breath. You bow from the ground and give up the seat.

events.text: By the sect's old rule the seat is settled by the nine elders' votes, and only if they split, by a duel. Elder Qiu tells you plainly: four votes are with the sibling who contests the seat, three with you, and two are for sale.

choices.text: Visit the two undecided elders with gifts (-120 taels).

effects.log: Elder Rao takes the ginseng and Elder Ping takes the inkstone. Neither promises anything. (-120 taels)

choices.text: Visit them with nothing but your plans for the sect.

ok.log: Elder Ping reads your plan for the lower halls twice and asks to keep it.

fail.log: Elder Rao falls asleep halfway through your plan.

choices.text: Do not canvass. Train for the duel instead.

effects.log: You spend the month on the cliff with your sword and nobody's opinion.

events.text: The nine elders vote with white and black stones in a bronze bowl. Elder Qiu counts them in front of the whole sect: four white, four black. Elder Ping holds the ninth stone and looks at you.

choices.text: Meet Elder Ping's eyes and wait.

ok.log: The ninth stone is white. The sect bows, unevenly at first, then together. The seat is yours.

fail.log: Elder Ping drops the stone back in his sleeve. 'Let them fight,' he says.

choices.text: Ask Elder Ping to abstain. Let the duel decide.

effects.log: The disciples cheer. They wanted a duel all along.

events.text: The duel is on the cliff plaza at noon, before the whole sect and the nine elders. The sibling who contests the seat draws first. Old Elder Qiu raises the bronze bowl, and drops it.

roll.foeName: the sibling who contests the seat

ok.log: A hundred breaths, then one. Your blade stops a finger from their throat. The seat is yours.

fail.log: Your sword rings on the stones. You bow, and the seat goes to the one still holding a blade.

choices.text: Fight to show the sect what you are, and stop at the first touch.

ok.log: You touch their sleeve, lower your sword and bow. The elders vote again, nine white stones.

fail.log: They touch you first, and the elders call for a second duel next month.

choices.text: Lay your sword down. The sect should not watch its heirs bleed.

effects.log: You give up the seat on the cliff. The younger disciples remember that for the rest of their lives.

events.text: Three factions kneel before your throne and none of them means it. The Crimson Banner wants war on the Martial Alliance, the Shadow Hall wants the Alliance's ledgers, and the Gold Lotus wants peace and the salt roads. Each brings a gift in a lacquer box.

choices.text: Open the Crimson Banner's box first.

effects.log: Inside: the seal of an Alliance captain. The Crimson Banner roars. The Gold Lotus goes very quiet.

choices.text: Open the Gold Lotus's box first.

effects.log: Inside: a salt licence and a great deal of silver. The Crimson Banner stops kneeling. (+150 taels)

choices.text: Open none of them. Thank all three and dismiss them.

ok.log: Three factions leave the hall each sure the others have bought you. That is exactly where you want them.

fail.log: All three factions decide you are weak. The whispering begins.

events.text: Shadow Hall Master Yan, who wears no mask because her face is already unreadable, asks for a private audience. 'The Crimson Banner will move against you at the Lantern Festival,' she says. 'For a price, they will not.'

choices.text: Pay her price: the Shadow Hall's choice of the next elder.

effects.log: Master Yan bows. You can feel the throne get a little smaller.

choices.text: Thank her and arrest the Crimson Banner's captains before the festival.

ok.log: The captains are dragged before the throne in chains by dawn. The Cult remembers who sits on it.

fail.log: Two captains escape into the hills with half the Crimson Banner behind them.

choices.text: Ask her why she is warning you, of all people.

ok.log: 'Because the last three Heavenly Demons did not ask,' she says. It is the beginning of a strange friendship.

fail.log: She smiles. 'Because I am paid to,' she says, and names her price anyway.

events.text: The Lantern Festival comes. Ten thousand red lanterns hang from the cliffs of the Cult's mountain, and somewhere under them the three banners are watching each other, and you.

choices.text: Walk among the lanterns alone, unguarded, so they all see you.

ok.log: One assassin, one blow, one lantern knocked down. After that the factions kneel and mean it.

fail.log: The assassin's blade finds your ribs. You walk on to the end of the lanterns anyway. That is remembered.

choices.text: Give each banner a festival task, far from the others.

effects.log: The Crimson Banner guards the north gate, the Gold Lotus counts the silver, the Shadow Hall watches both. Nobody has time to plot.

choices.text: Stay inside and let the factions burn each other out.

effects.log: By morning there are two banners, not three. You did not lift a finger, and everyone knows it.

events.text: A year after the Lantern Festival, Master Yan brings you the Cult's ledgers. For the first time in living memory, the three banners have paid their tribute on the same day.

choices.text: Name a fourth banner of your own, loyal only to the throne.

effects.log: The Black Lantern Banner is raised in the throne hall. The other three kneel very straight.

choices.text: Melt the three banners' silver into one throne treasury.

effects.log: The factions grumble, but they grumble together now, which is a kind of unity. (+200 taels)

events.text: Chancellor Wen Daoyuan kneels too long at morning court. That night a eunuch brings you a letter in Wen's hand, addressed to one of your grown children: 'The old dragon tires. When the time comes, the guards are ours.'

choices.text: Burn the letter and watch the chancellor closely.

effects.log: You burn it in your own brazier. Wen Daoyuan bows lower than ever the next morning.

choices.text: Have the chancellor arrested at dawn.

ok.log: Wen Daoyuan is taken from his bed. His papers name nine ministers and no children of yours, which is either the truth or very careful.

fail.log: Wen Daoyuan is warned. By dawn his house is empty and so are his papers.

choices.text: Send for the child the letter was addressed to.

effects.log: Your child reads the letter, goes white, and swears they never answered it. You have heard many oaths. This one might be true.

events.text: The ministers press you at every audience to name a crown heir. Each of your grown children has a faction, and every faction has a rumour about the others. The palace has started counting your coughs.

choices.text: Proclaim an open trial: each candidate governs a province for a year.

effects.log: The court is aghast, then fascinated. The candidates set out for the provinces with very different expressions.

choices.text: Let the factions fight it out and name whoever is left standing.

effects.log: The palace becomes a quiet war of memorials, poisoned rumours and borrowed seals. You watch from the throne.

choices.text: Refuse to name anyone. You are not dead yet.

effects.log: The ministers go away unhappy. You feel ten years younger out of spite.

events.text: The provinces send their reports. The Yellow River dykes held where one of your children governed; grain prices fell where another did; a third province is in open revolt. The court waits, brushes wet.

choices.text: Name the heir before the ancestral temple of the dynasty.

effects.log: The edict is read at dawn in the Hall of Supreme Harmony. The new crown heir kneels; the others kneel behind.

choices.text: Give the trial another year. The revolt must be understood.

effects.log: The court groans. The revolt, it turns out, was Wen Daoyuan's last plot, not your child's fault.

events.text: After a year of memorials, poisoned rumours and borrowed seals, one faction stands. Its candidate comes to the throne room alone, kneels, and does not look sorry for anything.

choices.text: Name the survivor heir. That is how thrones are kept.

effects.log: The edict is read. The other children bow very carefully, and the court learns what kind of dynasty this is.

choices.text: Refuse to reward the scheming. Start again with a trial.

effects.log: You tear the edict and set a trial. The schemer wins it anyway, but the court sees how.

events.text: Of your grown children, two stand out. The clever one has doubled the rent books and frightened every tenant. The kind one has forgiven half the tenants' debts and is loved in every village. The house can have only one head.
events.arc: The Clever One and the Kind One

choices.text: Watch them both a while longer.

effects.log: You start taking long walks past the rent office and the village wells.

choices.text: Set them a test: each runs the house for one season.

effects.log: The servants start a quiet book on which season will be the better one. Nobody tells you.

choices.text: Ask old Tenant Guo, who has known them both since childhood.

effects.log: Guo scratches his head. 'The clever one counts the grain. The kind one counts the people. The house needs both counted, Head.'

events.text: A flood takes the low fields. The clever one has a plan: buy the drowned land cheap from the ruined tenants. The kind one has a plan too: open the granary to everyone, house and village alike.
events.arc: The Clever One and the Kind One

effects.log: The house grows by forty mu. The villages grow cold. (+150 taels)
The granary empties and the villages live. The house is poorer and much loved. (-60 taels)

choices.text: Make them write one plan together.

ok.log: After three days of shouting, they produce a plan: buy no land, open the granary, and charge the grain back at harvest, with no interest. It works.

fail.log: They stop speaking to each other. You open the granary yourself.

events.text: The new year comes. The tablets are dusted, the incense is bought, and the whole household knows that tonight you will say a name before the ancestors, after the third cup, when the dumplings are gone.
events.arc: The Clever One and the Kind One

choices.text: Hold a fair trial before the tablets and let the house see who wins.

effects.log: The trial is long and fair. The loser bows first, which you notice and remember.

choices.text: Name neither yet. Tell them both they will run it together until you die.

effects.log: Two heads, one house. It is terrible for a year and then, oddly, very good.

events.text: Years after the new year of the names, the clever one and the kind one come to you together. 'We have decided,' they say. 'The clever one will run the books. The kind one will run the house. Please stop worrying.'
events.arc: The Clever One and the Kind One

choices.text: Laugh and hand over the keys.

effects.log: You sleep better that year than in the twenty before it.

choices.text: Ask them to swear it before the tablets.

effects.log: They swear it. They keep it, mostly, which is better than most oaths.

events.text: You have no children, and the cousins have begun to measure the courtyard. Then the cook finds a boy of six asleep in the woodshed, a runaway from the flood country, who says his name is Little Pan and asks if you need someone to sweep.

choices.text: Take him in as a servant and see.

effects.log: Little Pan sweeps badly and reads every scrap of paper he sweeps up.

choices.text: Adopt him before the tablets the same week.

effects.log: The cousins are outraged. Little Pan does not understand the ceremony and bows to the wrong tablet. It is perfect.

choices.text: Give him a coat and send him to the temple orphanage (-10 taels).

effects.log: He goes, waving. The cousins go back to measuring the courtyard. (-10 taels)

events.text: Little Pan is twelve now, and has taught himself to keep the house accounts better than the steward. Cousin Fu Ming, who expected the house, has noticed. 'A woodshed brat,' he says at dinner, 'with our ancestors' name.'

choices.text: Adopt Little Pan formally, now, at the table.

effects.log: You stand, take Little Pan by the shoulder, and name him. Cousin Fu Ming leaves the table and the house.

choices.text: Pay for Little Pan to study in the county school (-80 taels).

effects.log: He comes first in his year and writes you a letter every week, in a very neat hand. (-80 taels)

choices.text: Tell Cousin Fu Ming the house will be his. Keep the peace.

effects.log: Fu Ming beams. Little Pan goes on keeping the accounts, a little more quietly.

events.text: Little Pan, grown now and calling himself Pan Wenzhi, stands before the ancestral tablets in the house's name. The cousins are all there to see if the ancestors object. The incense burns straight up.

effects.log: Pan Wenzhi bows to the right tablet this time. The house has an heir, and a good one.

choices.text: Hand him the seal, and the woodshed key too.

effects.log: He laughs, then cries. Every winter after that, a runaway or two sleeps in that woodshed, warm, with a bowl of rice.

events.text: Cousin Fu Ming has the house's promise, and Pan Wenzhi has the house's accounts. One evening Fu Ming asks you, not unkindly, what the woodshed boy will do when Fu Ming is head.

choices.text: Change your mind and adopt Pan Wenzhi after all.

effects.log: Fu Ming takes it badly, then less badly when Pan Wenzhi offers to keep his accounts too.

choices.text: Make Fu Ming promise to keep Pan Wenzhi as steward for life.

effects.log: Fu Ming promises. Pan Wenzhi keeps that house running for forty years, under a head who never once reads a ledger.

events.text: The child you meant to make heir has been seen at the Willow Pavilion every night, reading poems to wine merchants. This morning a book arrived: Forty Verses on Leaving Home. The author's name is a pen name. You know the hand.

effects.log: You read it twice. Verse eleven is about you. It is not unkind.

choices.text: Have every copy in the county bought up (-50 taels).

effects.log: The printer is delighted and prints a second edition. (-50 taels)
The readings move to the Plum Pavilion, which is smaller and louder.

events.text: At dinner, the would-be poet sets down the chopsticks. 'I do not want the seat,' comes the sentence, very fast, as if it has been practised in a mirror for years. 'I want to go to the capital and write.'

choices.text: Let them go, with your blessing and some silver (-100 taels).

effects.log: The cart leaves at dawn. The house is quieter, and somehow lighter. (-100 taels)

ok.log: They stay. They are a decent head-in-training and a sad one, and the poems keep coming, quieter.

fail.log: They leave anyway, at night, by the kitchen door, with the book.

choices.text: Make a bargain: run the house five years, then choose.

effects.log: Hands are clasped on it. You suspect you have both lost and won.

events.text: A letter comes from the capital. The poet heir's verses have been praised by a Hanlin scholar and copied onto the wall of a famous wine shop. At the bottom: 'Name someone else. Somebody who wants it. I will come home for the new year.'

choices.text: Hold a trial among the others for the seat.

effects.log: The trial is held. The new heir is named. At the new year, the poet reads a verse about it, and the whole house laughs.

choices.text: Write back a poem of your own.

ok.log: Your poem is bad and honest. It comes back with corrections and a drawing of a cat.

fail.log: Your poem is only bad. You get no corrections, only a very kind letter.

events.text: The five years, or the duty, have passed. The poet heir runs the house well, on time, with every ledger clean, and writes nothing at all any more. One night you find the old book of Forty Verses in the kitchen stove, half-burnt.

choices.text: Pull it out, and tell them to go.

effects.log: The poet goes to the capital at last, and you hold a fair trial for the seat among the others. Verse forty-one arrives that spring.

choices.text: Leave it. A house needs heads more than poets.

effects.log: The house prospers. The poems never come back. Sometimes you wonder about verse forty-one.

events.text: Thirty mu of land: twelve of it good black soil by the river, ten of it hillside, eight of it stones that grow only thistles and arguments. Your grown children all know these numbers by heart.

choices.text: Walk every field with them, one by one, and talk.

effects.log: Two days of walking. You learn which child loves the river and which one loves the hill.

choices.text: Call in a surveyor to measure it exactly (-30 taels).

effects.log: The surveyor finds thirty-one mu. Nobody had counted the ditch. (-30 taels)

choices.text: Keep it whole. One heir, one farm.

effects.log: Your words land on the table like a stone. Nobody eats much.

events.text: The old rule in the valley: the eldest divides, the youngest chooses first. Your grown children are looking at you to see if the old rule still holds in this house.

effects.log: The eldest divides so carefully it takes all winter. Every share is exactly as bad as every other.

choices.text: Divide it yourself, by who works which field best.

effects.log: The river goes to the one who loves the river. The thistles go to the one who loves arguments.

choices.text: Give each child the same land and the same stones, in strips.

effects.log: Everyone gets a strip of river, a strip of hill and a strip of thistle. The neighbours call it the Comb.

events.text: The land question is settled. What is left is the house itself, the old brick farmhouse with the date tree and the ancestors' tablets, which cannot be cut into strips.

choices.text: Hold a trial: whoever keeps the best field this year keeps the house.

effects.log: The harvest is the trial, and the whole valley watches it. The winner is named before the tablets.

choices.text: Keep the house in common, for everyone, forever.

effects.log: The house stays open to all of them. Every new year it is loud, crowded, and yours.

events.text: One farm, one heir. Two years after your words at the table, the grown children who got nothing have gone: one to the city, one to the army, one to a neighbour's land. The farm is big and quiet.

choices.text: Write to each of them and offer a strip after all.

effects.log: Two come back for the harvest. One writes that the army suits better. The quiet fills up a little.

choices.text: Hold a trial now for the one who stayed, so it is at least fair.

effects.log: There is only one candidate, so the trial is short and the feast is long.

events.text: It has been years since the seat went to the sibling who won it. You hear things: the old storehouse sold, the servants let go, the new head grown thin and short-tempered. A peddler swears the house is a step from ruin.
events.arc: The Seat That Went to Someone Else

effects.log: You feel something anyway. It does not have a good name.

choices.text: Send a letter, with no silver in it, only a question.

effects.log: The letter says: 'Is it true?' You do not sign it. You do not have to.

choices.text: Begin to buy up the house's debts, quietly, through a broker.

effects.log: Note by note, the house's debts come to you. (-80 taels)

events.text: A letter arrives, in a hand you know, on cheap paper with the house's old seal pressed crooked at the bottom: 'It is true. Please come.' Nothing else, not even a name.
events.arc: The Seat That Went to Someone Else

effects.log: The gate is the same gate. The person waiting at it is not the same person who took the seat.
The silver goes. A thank-you comes back, stiff and grateful. You never quite go. (-100 taels)

events.text: You hold half the house's debts now. The broker says one word from you and the house is yours at last, the seat with it, and the sibling who won it out on the road.
events.arc: The Seat That Went to Someone Else

effects.log: The house falls into your hands like ripe fruit. It does not taste as you expected. (+200 taels)

choices.text: Burn the notes before the broker's eyes.

effects.log: The notes go up in a single bright breath. The broker thinks you have lost your mind. You think you have found it.

events.text: Sitting in the old courtyard with the one who took the seat, you share a pot of plum tea, the same kind the house made when you were both children. Neither of you mentions the contest. Both of you think of nothing else.
events.arc: The Seat That Went to Someone Else

choices.text: Say it out loud: 'I forgive you.'

effects.log: They laugh, then cry, then laugh again. 'I was going to say that to you,' they say.

choices.text: Offer to help run the house again, as an equal.

effects.log: The house is hauled back from the edge together, in two years of hard work. (+60 taels)

events.text: The seat is yours. The morning after, the creditors arrive in a polite line: the rice merchant, the timber merchant, a temple, and a moneylender called Sun the Patient, who has been patient for eleven years and has stopped.

choices.text: Open the strongbox in front of them all.

effects.log: The strongbox holds a moth, a ring, and an IOU from your own grandfather. The creditors look at each other.

choices.text: Promise everyone everything, then work out the sums.

ok.log: They give you a year. Sun the Patient gives you a look.

fail.log: They give you a month, and stay for dinner.

choices.text: Pay Sun the Patient first (-150 taels).

effects.log: Sun counts it twice, nods once, and says he will remember this. (-150 taels)

events.text: The sibling who lost the seat sends a note from a comfortable inn in the next county, all smiles: 'Congratulations. I believe the debts come with it.' The rice merchant is at the gate again.

choices.text: Laugh, and send back a list of the debts with half marked in their name.

effects.log: The reply comes fast and is not polite. But half of it is paid by autumn.

choices.text: Sell the old summer pavilion to clear the rice and timber debts.

effects.log: The pavilion your grandparents built goes to a salt merchant's nephew. (+90 taels)

choices.text: Work it off: open the courtyard as an inn for the season.

effects.log: Travellers sleep in the ancestral courtyard. The ancestors, presumably, get used to it. (+60 taels)

events.text: Three years on, the last creditor crosses the house off his book. Sun the Patient comes to the gate himself, with a box of pears and the house's last paper, torn in half.

effects.log: He tells you that only two houses in the county have ever paid him in full. Yours, and the temple.

choices.text: Hang the torn paper in the ancestral hall.

effects.log: It hangs beside the tablets where every heir after you will see it. The seat is yours, and it is free.

events.text: You have been head long enough to know the sound of every complaint before it is spoken. Last night you dreamed of a hut above the clouds on Mount Qingcheng, a tea bush and nobody at all knocking.

choices.text: Begin to hand the daily work to your grown children.

effects.log: The first week is chaos. The second week, somebody else handles it, and you go fishing.

choices.text: Send a carpenter to the mountain to build the hut (-80 taels).

effects.log: The carpenter sends back a drawing: one room, one stove, one window facing east. (-80 taels)

choices.text: Dismiss the dream. The house needs you.

effects.log: You stay up late over the ledgers. The dream comes back three nights running.

events.text: Before the tablets, the household gathers. You hold the seal. The grown children who would be head are in the front row, and the hut is waiting on the mountain.

choices.text: Name an heir by a fair trial, then leave.

effects.log: The trial is held, the seal is given, and you are on the road by noon.

choices.text: Let them settle it among themselves, and leave before it is done.

effects.log: You go up the mountain with the shouting still in your ears. It fades by the third bend.

choices.text: Keep the seal one more year. Just one.

effects.log: The children sigh. The hut gathers moss.

events.text: On the mountain the tea bush has flowered, and you have learned the names of six birds and one fox. A letter climbs up to you with a woodcutter: the new head has a problem and wants your counsel.

choices.text: Write three lines of advice and send it down.

effects.log: The three lines are good. The new head follows two of them, which is also good.

choices.text: Send back a packet of tea and no advice at all.

effects.log: The new head works it out alone, and is better for it. You are better for not knowing what it was.

choices.text: Go down the mountain to sort it out yourself.

effects.log: You sort it out in a day and then cannot remember why you left. You climb back up, slower.

events.text: The Wen clan says your ancestors' grave hill is theirs, by a deed from a dynasty ago. Since the dispute began, green lights have been seen on the hill at night, and the village says the dead are angry. Whose dead, nobody agrees.

choices.text: Go up the hill at night yourself and look.

ok.log: The lights are lanterns, green-papered, carried by two Wen servants who drop them and run.

fail.log: Something green floats past your face and you fall down the hill. The village hears about it by morning.

choices.text: Pay a Daoist priest to quiet the dead (-40 taels).

effects.log: Master Qing chants for three nights. The lights stop. The Wen clan's servants sleep for the first time in weeks. (-40 taels)

choices.text: Take the deed dispute to the magistrate.

effects.log: The magistrate opens a new file, dusts off an old one, and asks for both families' records.

events.text: Old Wen Jiyu, head of the Wen clan, ninety and stubborn, sends word: he will meet you at the grave hill at the Qingming festival, when both families sweep their dead.

choices.text: Go, with brooms and offerings for both families' graves.

effects.log: You sweep a Wen grave beside your own. Old Wen Jiyu watches, then sweeps one of yours.

choices.text: Go with the green lanterns the servants dropped.

effects.log: You set the lanterns at Wen Jiyu's feet. He goes red, then grey, then very still.

choices.text: Send your strongest cousins, and stay home.

effects.log: The cousins and the Wen servants scuffle among the graves. Both families are ashamed by evening.

events.text: The magistrate has read the old records. The deed is real, but so is another older one: the hill was given to both families by a lord who loved them equally, five hundred years ago. Both lines have been sweeping each other's dead all along.

choices.text: Raise one stone for both families on the hill (-60 taels).

effects.log: The stone says nothing about deeds. It says: Two Houses, One Hill. The lights never come back. (-60 taels)

choices.text: Ask Old Wen Jiyu to dinner.

effects.log: He brings a jar of old wine and a story about your great-great-grandmother that nobody in your house has ever heard.

events.text: At the new year feast, two grandchildren are fighting over who sits in the carved chair at the head of the table. It is your chair. Nobody has noticed that you are standing in the doorway, holding a dish of dumplings.

effects.log: Both children leap out of the chair at once. Both claim they were keeping it warm for you.

choices.text: Watch and see how they settle it.

effects.log: The smaller one wins by bribing the bigger one with a dumpling. You recognise the family style.

choices.text: Set the dumplings down and sit on the floor with them.

effects.log: Within a minute the whole table is on the floor and nobody remembers the chair.

events.text: A grandchild comes to you privately, very serious, with a list written in big wobbly characters: reasons why the house should go to them one day. Reason six is 'I can whistle'.

choices.text: Read every reason gravely and give it a mark.

effects.log: The child goes away with 'six out of ten' and a determination that frightens you a little.

choices.text: Tell the child a house is not a prize.

effects.log: The child nods, does not believe a word of it, and goes off to practise whistling.

choices.text: Give the child a copper and send them to buy sweets for all the cousins.

effects.log: The child comes back with sweets for all the cousins and an alliance with three of them. (-1 taels)

events.text: Your grown children are watching the grandchildren squabble, and you can see it on their faces: they remember their own squabbles, and some of them have not forgiven a thing.

choices.text: Gather them all at the tablets and tell the old stories, including the shameful ones.

effects.log: There is a lot of laughter and some tears, and one long-held grudge is let go, right there before the incense.

choices.text: Write it down: how the seat will pass, and to whom, so there is nothing left to fight about.

effects.log: The paper goes behind the tablets, sealed. The grandchildren still fight over the chair, but only over the chair.

events.text: Disciple Han Yu is the best sword the sect has raised in sixty years, and an orphan from the salt marshes. Your grown children are good, not great. The elders say the seat should follow the blood. The disciples say it should follow the sword.

choices.text: Spar with Han Yu yourself to take the measure.

ok.log: You win, barely, and know you will never win again. Han Yu bows and thanks you for the lesson.

fail.log: Han Yu disarms you in nine moves and looks horrified about it.

choices.text: Watch your children teach the young disciples.

effects.log: Your children are patient and the young ones love them. Han Yu, watching, teaches no one.

choices.text: Ask the elders to put it to a vote.

effects.log: The elders vote five to four for blood. The disciples mutter in the halls.

events.text: Han Yu comes to your hall at night. 'I do not want your seat,' he says. 'I want to fight the Demonic Cult on the western border, and I want the sect behind me when I do.'

choices.text: Give Han Yu the western hall and a hundred disciples.

effects.log: Han Yu bows to the floor. The western border stops being a worry within three years.

choices.text: Ask Han Yu to stay and serve the next head instead.

effects.log: Han Yu stays, unhappily. He is very good at serving, which is the saddest thing about it.

events.text: The time has come. The seat goes to the blood, the elders have decided. But which of the blood, they leave to you, and the disciples are watching to see if you choose by sword or by name.

choices.text: Hold a fair trial among your children, with Han Yu as judge.

effects.log: Han Yu judges hard and fair. The winner is named before the founder's tablet, and the disciples cheer for the judge too.

choices.text: Let your children settle it however they like.
